2.0.0.en: If the soul had spoken with her relatives about the Lord Christ as her Bridegroom, praising His love and going on describing Him, and then returned and met with her betrothed the Good Shepherd, and came to know Him as a King who raises her up as a queen who sits with Him, now she goes down with Him to the garden, far from all affectation or formalities, conversing together in sweet talk.

2.0.1.en: He says to her: If the world has drawn you with all its enticements, so that you sought its pleasures and delights, then I come down to you into the world, and I am in the valleys within your reach, that you may know Me:

2.0.2.en: “I am the narcissus of Sharon, the lily of the valleys” [1].

2.0.3.en: Sharon is a plain in Judea, a very fertile region where water is available, but it was not cultivated, since it is a narrow place that was used as a road between Egypt and Syria. The narcissus of this plain is of an excellent kind, appearing without any man planting it or toiling in it. Thus our Beloved appears in our land; He came to us by His grace, and not for any righteousness in us.

2.0.4.en: And in the midst of the barren valleys the Lord appears as a lily, which St. Gregory of Nyssa describes as rising straight upward, its flower at the top far from the earth... Thus the Lord came to our barren valleys to lift us up by Him to above and to be for us the heavenly flower.

2.0.5.en: This expression came in the Septuagint thus: “I am the flower of the field (the plain), the lily of the valleys.” And Origen comments thus: [The field is a piece of land under cultivation, which the farmers plow, but the valleys are often stony lands that have not previously been cultivated. Thus we can understand by the field or the plain the people whom the Law and the prophets cultivated, and by the stony, unplowed valleys the Gentile peoples... Thus the Bridegroom appears as the flower among that people, for the Law made nothing perfect (Heb 7:19), since the word of God (in the Old Testament) could not advance them to be a flower, nor bring them to the perfection of fruit. And in the valleys, which are the community of the Gentiles, He became the lily].

2.0.6.en: The Lord Christ is the flower of the Jewish people, for the Law led to Christ, and He is the lily of the Gentile peoples since they accepted Him as Savior... He is the Christ of the whole world: Jews and Gentiles.

2.0.7.en: St. Jerome sees that the flower of the field or the lily of the wilderness (the valleys) is the person of the Messiah who budded in Aaron’s rod, the flower that sprang up in St. Mary, who, although in herself she carries no life, bore “Life” itself.

2.0.8.en: He says also: [The saying that He came from (the wilderness) refers to the Virgin who presented God to us in a form without bodily relationship or human seed... so we sing with the words of the psalm: “as in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is, so have I appeared unto thee in the sanctuary” (Ps 63:1-2)].

2.0.9.en: And St. Ambrose says: [Mary is the rod, and Christ is the flower of Mary, the sweet fragrance of faith in whom spreads in the whole world, as He appears as a bud in the virginal womb, for He said of Himself: “I am the flower of the plain or the lily of the valleys” [1].

2.0.10.en: When a flower is plucked it keeps its fragrance, and when it is crushed its scent increases, and if it is cut into pieces it does not lose its fragrance. So also when the Lord Jesus was hung on the Cross He did not fail when He was crushed, nor weaken when He was torn, and when He was pierced by the spear He became more beautiful by the blood poured out of Him, as though He had carried a new beauty that cannot die in itself (a spiritual death) but gives the dead the gift of eternal life. And the Holy Spirit rested upon this flower that budded in the royal rod].

2.1.0.en: This is our Beloved to us, His bride; He has carried by His sufferings the sweet fragrance, smelled by those in the plain, that is the Jews, and those in the valley, that is the community of the Gentiles... But what are we to Him?

2.1.1.en: “As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters” [2].

2.1.2.en: Origen says: [Since He became the lily of the valleys, it was that His beloved also might become a lily imitating Him... that is, every soul that draws near to Him and follows His steps and imitates Him becomes a lily].

2.1.3.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa sees that the soul like the lily rises straight upward toward the Messiah her true Vinedresser. He lifts her above the cares of this life and the thorns of sin that choke the soul (Mk 4:18), and rises above the dust of this life that she may not be defiled...

2.1.4.en: The believer in the eyes of the Lord is like the lily, “the lily-flower,” exceedingly splendid, and not even Solomon in all his glory was arrayed like it, beautiful not by her own righteousness but by the grace of the blood that runs in her...

2.1.5.en: Though man has accepted the thorns of sin, so that they surround him on every side, yet the Lord sees him as the lily, comes down to him and passes through the midst of the thorns, and bears the curse for him!

2.1.6.en: In the Beloved’s address, “As the lily among thorns,” there is also guidance to her that if she wants to be adorned with virtues she must bear the pains of the thorns with care, and as St. Ambrose says: [The virtues are surrounded by thorns of spiritual evil, so that no one can gather the fruit unless he draws near with care].

2.1.7.en: Origen sees in this saying a true picture of the beautiful Church surrounded by heresies and heretics who want to destroy her...

2.1.8.en: St. Augustine sees in this expression and its like a declaration of the fewness of the righteous who live in the midst of the world “like a lily among many thorns” until the day of harvest comes and separates the lilies from the thorns.

2.2.0.en: Though the human soul has become like a lily among thorns, she is not occupied with the thorns around her, but with the Bridegroom who satisfies her and waters her and gives her fragrance... She sees Him coming to her, drawing near to her that she may draw near to Him, lifted up on the Cross that she may rest in the shade of His eternal love, and He presents to her the fruit of the Cross, sweetness in her throat; therefore she addresses Him, saying:

2.2.1.en: “As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved among the sons. I desired to sit under his shadow, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” [3].

2.2.2.en: Though she lives among the thorns and cannot rise to Him, He comes down to her, and becomes like the apple tree (a symbol of the divine Incarnation) within her reach. He has dwelt among us, the fruitless thicket, and became one of us, but not fruitless like us, but like the apple tree: beautiful to see, its fragrance refreshing, its fruit eaten, and its juice drunk... He is the tree of life that we pluck instead of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

2.2.3.en: Truly, the earth has been dry for such a length of time, because we ate from the tree of disobedience, and the Beloved came, “the obedient Son”... He came to us in the midst of our thorns, and entered into our sufferings, and bore the curse of the thorns for us, that we may sit at His feet and take shelter under the Cross of His love in the midst of the severity of the distress of this world.

2.2.4.en: In the world there are many trees of the thicket that we imagine to be restful for us, but one tree—the spiritual apple tree—has in it all satisfaction.

2.2.5.en: If “the apple tree” refers to the divine Incarnation, then the trees of the thicket refer to heresies and strange teachings, for there is no rest for us except in the incarnate Word alone, far from every heresy. In this Origen says: [The bride desires to sit under the shade of this apple tree, meaning that the Church, as we said, is under the protection of the Son of God, or that the soul flees from all strange teachings to cleave to the Word of God alone and finds His fruit sweet in her throat, through continual meditation on the law of God, chewing it as though she ruminates it as the clean animal does].

2.2.6.en: In ancient times the Gentiles sat in the shadow of death (Isa 9:2; Mt 4:16) as they sat under the shadow of the tree of disobedience, but now they enjoy the shadow of the Giver of life by sitting under the shadow of the Cross of obedience.

2.2.7.en: In ancient times the Jews sat under the shadow of the Law, through the literal, killing understanding. But now it has been given to us to enter under the shadow of Christ by tasting the spiritual understanding of the Law which edifies. And the following is a comparison by Origen between the shadow of the Law and the shadow of Christ:

2.2.8.en: [It seems that every soul as long as it is in this present life needs a shade, as I think because of the heat of the sun which makes the seed without deep roots wither and die. The shadow of the Law gave a little protection against this heat, but the shadow of Christ under which the Gentiles now live—that is, faith in the Incarnation—gives complete protection from the heat and even extinguishes it. For (Satan), who used to burn the poor who were under the shadow of the Law, was seen falling from heaven like lightning at the time of the passion of Christ. But the time of this shadow is completed at the end of the ages, for as we said, at the end of time we no longer see (Christ) in a mirror nor in a riddle, but face to face].

2.2.9.en: St. Mary, who represents the Church, as an ideal member in her, sat under the shadow of the Most High through the divine Incarnation, as the angel said to her: “the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God...” By this it has become possible for the believer to sit under the shadow of the Lord and eat His sweet fruit after his mouth had been embittered for a time of such length because of sin. After it was said of himself, “their throat is an open sepulchre” (Ps 5:11), she has come to open her mouth not as a sepulchre bearing the death of sin but rather to eat the Body of the Son of God the Giver of life, and to taste the sweetness of His fruit... She says also: [I opened my mouth, and drew to myself a spirit] (Ps 119:131).

2.2.10.en: Origen says: [Her saying “and his fruit was sweet to my throat” applies to the soul in whose mouth there is nothing dead or base, and who does not at all resemble those of whom it was said (their throat is an open sepulchre); for such mouths that bring out words of death and perdition are called sepulchres, those that utter words contrary to the true faith, and oppose the order of purity and justice and dignity].

2.3.s.en: In the house of perfect love:

2.3.0.en: When the soul sits with her Beloved at the Cross, and tastes His infinite love, she asks Him to enter into His bowels to be watered from the deep springs of His love, saying:

2.3.1.en: “He brought me to the house of wine, and his banner over me was love. Stay me with cakes of raisins, comfort me with apples: for I am wounded with love” [4-5].

2.3.2.en: We have already seen that “the house of wine” is the house of “the new life” that became ours through the saving sufferings of the Lord Christ. The house of wine symbolizes “the house of the feast and of wisdom,” where the soul enters to the Lord Christ and receives the juice of the teachings of truth and its mixture in the vessel of divine wisdom, by which the soul is refreshed anew every day... as she comes to know the mysteries of God as though they were new every day.

2.3.3.en: In this Origen says: [As for the wine that is extracted from the true Vine, “the Lord Christ,” it is always new, by which the understanding of the learners of spiritual knowledge and wisdom is renewed continually; for this reason Jesus said to His disciples: I will drink this wine with you new in my Father’s kingdom (Mt 26:29), because the understanding of hidden things and the declaration of mysteries is continually renewed through the wisdom of God, and that not only for men, but also for the angels and heavenly powers].

2.3.4.en: When the loving Lord brings the believing soul into the house of His love and reveals to her the mysteries of His wisdom that are new every day, she understands “love” as a sign of the victory of her Beloved and King, so she sets up “the banner of victory” over her, saying: “his banner over me was love.” He has reigned over her completely by love. But the Septuagint’s rendering of this expression came thus:

2.3.6.en: When the soul enters the house of her Beloved she is bound by the law of His house, namely “love,” but since she cannot apply it by herself she asks Him to Himself arrange the life of love in her, that is, she receives from God “true love,” the law of His love, so she knows how to love God and parents and brothers... and so on.

2.3.7.en: Love has its own ordering: man is bound to love God with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his might... that is, to love without reckoning and without limits. And man is bound to love his neighbor as himself (for its salvation), and his love for his brother would be a love that has lost its good ordering. Man is bound to love his parents by honoring them practically in the Lord, as a husband is bound to love his wife in a way that differs from the love of children for parents, and different from the love of shepherds for their people. Truly in “the house of love” we receive the one nature of love from its Source, “God Himself,” but we are bound also to come to know the law of practical love.

2.3.8.en: The soul returns to cry out, declaring her need of “love,” saying:

2.4.0.en: “Stay me with cakes of raisins (spices), comfort me with apples: for I am wounded with love” [5].

2.4.1.en: Since the soul has entered “the house of divine love” and received from God the ordering of love, she declares that she has become wounded with love; it is impossible for these wounds to be those of a bodily love, for according to Eastern traditions it is not fitting for the beloved to say that she is wounded with love but for the man alone. And besides, how could the beloved ask others—other than her Beloved—to support her or comfort her?! Can cakes of raisins or spices or apples bind up the wounds of love or heal its sickness?

2.4.2.en: These are the cries of the soul within the Church, “the house of love,” as she asks the servants of Christ to support her with cakes of raisins or the spices which are the comforting divine teachings that pour the love of Christ within and spread His sweet fragrance. She asks for the apple which is a symbol of the holy Body, for it is the mystery of her spiritual refreshment! For it alone can satisfy the heart with love, and give the soul a good and fitting ordering of love.

2.4.3.en: As for the secret of the soul’s wounds by love, as Origen says it is Christ Himself, who is the living and effective word of God, sharper than a two-edged sword, who enters into the depths of the soul and wounds her with divine love; and the following are some comments of the Fathers on this expression.

2.4.4.en: * Would that the unhealthy be wounded, for when they are wounded as is fitting they become healthy!

2.4.5.en: St. Augustine * Holy Scripture teaches us that God is love (1 Jn 4:8); He aimed His only-begotten Son, “the chosen arrow” (Isa 49:2), at the chosen, planting its threefold point in the spirit of life.

2.4.6.en: The head of the arrow is faith, which binds the one who shoots the arrow with those struck by it, as though the soul is lifted by divine elevators, so she sees within her the arrow of sweet love wounding her. Adorned with wounds...

2.4.7.en: It is a good wound and a sweet pain, by which “life” penetrates the soul. For by means of the tears of the “arrow” the soul opens the door that is her entrance...

2.4.8.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa * If anyone is ever set ablaze with sincere love for the word of God, if he has received one of the sweet wounds of this “chosen arrow” as the prophet calls it, if anyone has been wounded by the spear of His knowledge, worthy of all love, so that he yearns and longs for Him night and day, so that he can speak of no one but Him, nor listen to any but Him, nor think of anything but Him, nor incline to any desire or hope for any other, when it becomes thus the soul says truly: “I am wounded with love.” She receives her wound from the One of whom she says: “He hath made me a chosen arrow, and in his quiver hath he hid me” (Isa 49:2).

2.4.9.en: It is fitting for God to strike our souls with a wound like this, to wound them with such arrows and spears, to strike them with such healing wounds...

2.4.10.en: Since God is “love,” they say of themselves: “I am wounded with love.” Truly it is the drama of love when the soul says: I have received the wounds of love!

2.4.11.en: The soul that is set ablaze with longing for the wisdom of God, that is, that can behold the beauty of His wisdom, says in the same way: “I am wounded with wisdom.” And the soul that contemplates the loftiness of His power and is amazed at the power of His word can say: “I am wounded with power.” I think that such a soul is the very one that said: “The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?” (Ps 26). And the soul that is set ablaze with love of the justice of God and contemplates the justice of the ordering of His providence says truly: “I am wounded with justice.” And the soul that looks to the greatness of His goodness and the tenderness of His love speaks likewise. But the wound that includes all these things is the wound of love by which the bride declares: “I am wounded with love.”

2.5.0.en: These are the wounds of love with which the soul was wounded by “the chosen arrow,” the Lord Christ, who by His love places His left hand under our heads that He may direct them away from temporal things, cutting off in us all love for earthly things, and with His right hand draws us toward heavenly things; therefore the soul addresses Him thus:

2.5.1.en: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand doth embrace me” [6].

2.5.2.en: In other words, with His left hand He disciplines, so that temporal life and all the pleasures of the body and the world become small before us, and with His right hand He shows mercy, as He opens the heart before the heavenly things so that we long for them. In any case, the Lord places His disciplines under our heads, for without them our heads would not be balanced, and surrounds our heads with His right hand so that our hearts are filled with hope in Him! These are the true, healing divine wounds of love.

2.6.0.en: When the soul entered into the house of divine love, and was wounded by the healing arrow, she feels His infinite love whether in His disciplines or His tenderness, and feels through both (discipline and tenderness) as though her head were leaning on His left hand and encircled by His right hand, so her whole being is in His divine embrace while her face is opposite His face, receiving all the kisses of His divine mouth... therefore she is careful that no one cut off these deep fellowships, saying:

2.6.1.en: “I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and by the hinds (powers) of the fields, that ye stir not up, nor awake the beloved, till he please...” [7].

2.6.2.en: It is as though she carried the feelings of the Apostle Peter when his depths were wholly drawn toward the Lord Christ transfigured before him, and he said: “Lord, it is good for us to be here” (Mt 17:4).

2.6.3.en: Certainly, this expression cannot apply to bodily love, for how would the beloved ask her friends not to wake the beloved?! Is this their work? But it is a wonderful picture of the Church the Mother who asks her children, “the daughters of Jerusalem,” to remain in the divine embrace, and not to disturb the Lord who rests in their hearts by committing evil or sin! It is the voice of the Church the Mother toward every believing soul called “a daughter of Jerusalem” who looks to the heavenly Jerusalem as her mother, adjuring her by the powers of her inner field which the Lord blessed! (Gen 27:27), as she is the Lord’s husbandry (1 Cor 3:9), to remain embracing the divine love that dwells in her.

2.6.4.en: And perhaps it is also the voice of the Church directed to the community of the Jews, “the daughters of Jerusalem,” who saw the Messiah sleeping on the Cross, buried in the tomb, that they not be disturbed by this and deny faith in Him, for although He appeared as though in weakness, He rises when He pleases, on the third day. He slept on the Cross by His will, and rises also by His will, for He says:

2.6.5.en: “I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again,” but alas, the Jews refused to accept the crucified Lord Christ, awaiting a messiah according to the desires of their hearts.

2.7.0.en: 1. He comes down to her Himself. 2. He warns her of the slanderers. 3. The wedding banquet.

2.8.s.en: He comes down to her Himself

2.8.0.en: “The voice of my beloved (my sister’s son)! behold, he cometh triumphant upon the mountains, leaping upon the hills. My beloved (my sister’s son) is like a roe or a young hart: behold, he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows, flashing through the lattices” [8-9].

2.8.1.en: The Church of the Gentiles speaks with the Jewish people in gentle reproach, saying to them: I have come to know “the Word of God,” or the voice of the Beloved, who came incarnate through the Jews (my sister’s son); I knew Him through the mountains of the Law that you received and the hills of the prophecies that are in your hands. He came to me triumphantly with joy and gladness through the Law and the prophecies, but in the fullness of time He came to me Himself like the roe, carrying our nature, hiding behind it—standing behind our wall—speaking with us directly.

2.8.2.en: I received the message of His Incarnation through the windows of the Law and the lattices of the prophets... I knew His voice and was able to distinguish it (Jn 10:3-4).

2.8.3.en: In this St. Gregory of Nyssa says: [The brightness (of the Word) reached the Church by way of the prophets first. Finally, by the proclamation of the Gospel the shadows of the types vanished completely and the dividing wall was torn down, and the atmosphere of the inner house was joined to the light of the heights of heaven; there was no more need for the light of the windows since the true light had illumined all the inside with the rays of the Gospel].

2.9.0.en: If the Church had come to know the incarnate Word of God through the law of the Old Testament and the prophecies, the speech here comes as a call directed to every soul to rise by the Holy Spirit upon the mountains of Holy Scripture to meet there the Suitor who comes to betroth His betrothed. Therefore the psalmist says: “His foundation is in the holy mountains,” “I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help” (Ps 86:1; 120:1).

2.9.1.en: Origen sees that the soul that wants to meet with “the Word of God,” who is triumphant on the mountains, leaping on the hills in perfect freedom, must meet Him on the bare mountains of the books of the New Testament and upon the hills of the books of the Old Testament which remained for a long time hidden and not perceived.

2.9.2.en: In the book of Jeremiah we find the Lord sending hunters and fishers to catch men on every mountain and upon every hill (Jer 16:16), as though it were a prophecy of the preaching work of the Church, where the Church catches souls through Holy Scripture to enjoy the blessings of salvation.

2.9.3.en: On these holy mountains souls meet the Word of God, and see Him as the Suitor who asks for her hand. There she hears the voice of His call to her, so she experiences His love and His divine mysteries are unveiled and she beholds His glory.

2.9.4.en: As though the soul rises with Moses the prophet on Mount Horeb and sees the bush burning with fire and not consumed (Ex 3:2), she perceives the mystery of the divine Incarnation, as she sees the Virgin Mary (the bush) bearing the coal of divinity and not consumed...

2.9.5.en: I say that she also ascends with Moses on the mountain to receive the divine Law, not engraved on two tablets of stone, but with the Word of God Himself dwelling in her heart!

2.9.6.en: Or as though she sits with the crowds to see her Jesus ascending the mountain, opening His mouth and speaking with her directly and without barriers (Mt 5:1), or she ascends with Him on Mount Tabor that He may be transfigured before her and she perceives the brightness of His divinity and hears Him speak with Moses and Elijah about the matters concerning the events of her salvation. Or as though she climbs with “the Word of God” on the mount of temptation, to see Him tempted and conquering for her sake!

2.9.7.en: By this the believing soul understands why the Lord Christ called Himself the stone cut out of the mountain without hands, which became a great mountain (Dan 2:43), and why the Church also was called Mount Zion, as an indication of the dwelling of God who dwells on high with His people. She listens to the saying of the two angels to Lot: “Escape for thy life... escape to the mountain, lest thou be consumed” (Gen 19:17).

2.10.s.en: She likens Him to the roe and the young harts:

2.10.0.en: To what does the bride liken her betrothed?

2.10.1.en: “My beloved (my sister’s son) is like a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of Beth-el” [9]. 1. The Lord Christ is likened to the roe (the gazelle), and the word “roe” in Hebrew means “beauty,” for the Lord Christ came seeking the hand of humanity which sin had corrupted and disfigured in its inner nature and spiritual beauty, to be united with it and pour His beauty upon it. And the Lord summarized this wonderful saving work in a speech of reproach to humanity, in which He said: “And I passed by thee, and saw thee trodden in thine own blood, and I said unto thee, In thy blood live.... I have caused thee to multiply as the bud of the field, and thou hast increased and waxen great, and thou art come to excellent ornaments: thy breasts are fashioned, and thine hair is grown, whereas thou wast naked and bare. Now when I passed by thee, and looked upon thee, behold, thy time was the time of love; and I spread my skirt over thee, and covered thy nakedness: yea, I sware unto thee, and entered into a covenant with thee, saith the Lord GOD, and thou becamest mine. Then washed I thee with water; yea, I throughly washed away thy blood from thee, and I anointed thee with oil. I clothed thee also with broidered work, and shod thee with badgers’ skin, and I girded thee about with fine linen, and I covered thee with silk. I decked thee also with ornaments, and I put bracelets upon thy hands, and a chain on thy neck. And I put a ring in thy nose, and earrings in thine ears, and a beautiful crown upon thine head. Thus wast thou decked with gold and silver; and thy raiment was of fine linen, and silk, and broidered work; thou didst eat fine flour, and honey, and oil: and thou wast exceeding beautiful, and thou didst prosper into a kingdom. And thy renown went forth among the heathen for thy beauty: for it was perfect through my comeliness, which I had put upon thee, saith the Lord GOD” (Ezek 16:6-14).

2.10.2.en: Truly how wonderful is the speech of the Lord the Savior toward the Church whom He joined to Himself after He passed by her and found her cast on the road naked and trodden in her blood, so He sanctified her completely. He spread His skirt over her, that is, He betrothed her as a bride to Himself, and covered her shame and nakedness with His blood, washed her with the water of Baptism and anointed her with the oil of the Myron, and clothed her with His life, and gave her His Gospel, the mystery of her salvation, adorned her with the works of the Holy Spirit, and placed His holy yoke as a collar on her neck, and spread His sweet fragrance that her nose smells, and sanctified her ears and adorned them by hearing the divine promises and the heavenly hymns, and satisfied her with the heavenly Bread, and in short made her “exceeding beautiful,” so she deserved to be a queen, reflecting the splendor of the Savior in her life.

2.10.3.en: In this St. John Chrysostom says:

2.10.4.en: [As I said, that He who is great and mighty desired a harlot, and I am speaking of human nature under that name: (harlot).

2.10.5.en: If a man desires a harlot he is condemned; how then does God desire a harlot to be a bridegroom to her?! What does He do? He did not send to her one of His servants, not an angel nor an archangel nor cherubim nor seraphim, but came down Himself, He who loves her, drawing near to her... He does not lead her as a harlot to the heights, for He does not want to bring a harlot into heaven, but He Himself came down to her. So as long as she is unable to ascend to the heights, He came down on the earth. He came to the harlot and was not ashamed to take hold of her while she was in her drunkenness...].

2.10.6.en: In other words, the Lord came to us “as a roe” to make of us a beautiful and perfect doe able to live on the heights (the heavenly places), as the psalmist says: “who perfecteth my feet like hinds’ feet, and setteth me upon high places.” 2. And St. Augustine comments on this, saying: [He makes my love perfect, so that it rises above the nets of this world full of thorns and darkness. He sets me upon the high places, and fixes my aim toward the heavenly dwelling that I may be filled with the fulness of God (Eph 3:19)]. 3. Origen sees that the word “roe” in Greek came from the sharpness of its sight, and he comments on that, saying: [And who can see as Christ sees? For He alone sees the Father or knows Him. For although it is said of the pure in heart that they see God, yet they see Him through the revelation of Christ to them (Jn 6:6; Mt 5:8). For it is of the nature of the roe not only to see and perceive accurately but also to give others the ability to see... Therefore Christ is compared to the roe or the gazelle, since He not only sees the Father but makes Him visible to those to whom He gives healing of their sight. But it is fitting for you not to take the speech about “seeing the Father” in any bodily understanding, or suppose that God is as it were visible. For God is not seen by bodily sight, but by the sight of the mind and the spirit... Finally, He gives those to whom He gives the power of seeing God the spirit of knowledge and the spirit of wisdom, so that by this Spirit they behold God; therefore He told His disciples: “he that hath seen me hath seen the Father” (Jn 14:9)]. 4. The roe and the hart are known for swiftness of foot (2 Sam 2:18; 1 Kgs 12:8), for the incarnate Word of God, although He came to us in the last times, that is, thousands of years after the fall, yet this does not mean that God was slow in our salvation... but He was hastening to prepare salvation, running toward us until He came down to us in the fullness of time; He hastened to us before we sought Him or searched for Him. 5. St. Augustine sees in the hart not only swiftness of movement with all its energies, but that in its running it thirsts and so runs toward the water brooks. And on the way it kills snakes and so its thirst for the water brooks increases more than before. Therefore the psalmist says: “As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God” (Ps 42:1).

2.10.7.en: If the believers gather together in one spirit like one hart longing for the water brooks of the love of God, then the Son of God truly came to us like the hart, thirsting for “our love”... and on the way of our salvation He shattered the old serpent, the devil, because of His love in us. 6. It is of the habits of the hart to leap on the rocks (2 Sam 22:34; Hab 3:19), for the Suitor who came to us did not seek the easy way but hastened to the sufferings with joy for our salvation. And as the Apostle Paul says: “Looking unto the author and finisher of our faith... who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame” (Heb 12:2). 7. According to the Mosaic law, the roe and the hart were among the holy animals, whose eating was permitted (Deut 12:22; 14:5)... Therefore the likeness to the roe and the hart was chosen, because the Suitor, as He stretches out His hand to His bride, offers His most holy Body and Blood as a dowry for her, the mystery of her sanctification and her eternity! 8. As the Suitor was likened to the hart, so His betrothed who carried His features was likened also to the hart, for it is said of her in the book of Psalms: “The voice of the LORD perfecteth the harts and discovereth the rough places” (Ps 29:9). And in the speech of the Lord with Job in the tempest through the cloud He said to him: “Knowest thou the time when the wild goats of the rock bring forth? or canst thou mark when the hinds do calve (the travail of the harts)? Canst thou number the months that they fulfil? or knowest thou the time when they bring forth? They bow themselves, they bring forth their young ones (give birth), they cast out their sorrows (their travail). Their young ones are in good liking, they grow up in the wilderness; they go forth, and return not unto them” (Job 39:1).

2.10.8.en: Origen comments on the two preceding texts, saying: [Since the speech here is about spiritual harts, the “voice of the LORD,” who is Christ the Word of God, is the One who gives the harts the life of perfection (Ps 29:9)... He is the secret of her perfection. As for the Lord’s speech with Job concerning the harts, here the Lord affirms His personal care for the souls of the believers; He cares for the months of their spiritual pregnancy, and when they give birth to virtues, and cares for her young, raises them and feeds them... as though God, who in the Song of Songs was likened to the hart, in His turn likens us to the hart and to our inner life and our virtues, that is, our conduct in Christ Jesus.

2.10.9.en: And in the book of Proverbs the wife is likened to the hart and her children to the wild goat... as an image of the Church, the true bride, the wife who loves the Lord her Bridegroom and is full of grace... Therefore it was said: “Let her be unto thee a loving hind and a graceful wild goat” (Prov 5:19). 9. As for His likeness to the young harts, it is an affirmation of the Incarnation, for the unlimited God became a child by His Incarnation, emptying Himself of everything for our sake. 10. His likeness to the hart reminds us of what came as the title of the twenty-second psalm, “To the chief musician upon the hind of the morning,” the psalm that describes the events of the Crucifixion and the Resurrection in some detail; and what is meant by the hind of the morning but the new life that the Savior (who is like the hart) presented to us by His Resurrection on the morning of Sunday?!

2.10.10.en: And He came triumphant on the mountains, leaping on the hills, to bring His betrothed into the power of the Resurrection, that is, to receive the new life that became hers in Christ Jesus, and as the Apostle Paul says: “raised us up together with him in the heavenly places” (Eph 2:6). 11. Finally, His mention of “the mountains of Beth-el” refers to the Holy Scriptures that belong to the house of God (El), that is, the Church, for we cannot experience the beauty of the Lord nor receive His Incarnation and Resurrection and His work in us except through the Church (the house of God)!

2.11.0.en: 1. When the Savior came down to us seeking us as a bride for Himself, He came to us from heaven and came down even to our wall that we built by our disobedience to God. He came to the veil that separated us from the Holy of Holies of God and stood behind it working and striving unto blood, and shattered it, and opened for us a heavenly way in which we walk.

2.11.1.en: We built the veil, so we became unable to ascend to Him; therefore He came down to us, and on the Cross the veil of the temple was torn, that He may shine upon us by His Resurrection through the windows and lattices that He made Himself. 2. And “our wall” also refers to our human nature, for He came down to us hidden behind our humanity so that we would not be terrified of Him or fear Him, but accept Him and love union with Him.

2.12.0.en: The Suitor came down to the house of His betrothed knowing that many nets and snares had been set for her that make her unable to go out of her house alone and rise to His house... He Himself came down, He alone whom the snares of sin cannot hold nor the nets of death catch, for He trod sin under His feet and by His life-giving death trampled death and shattered it in its own home... And now He calls His betrothed to come out with Him and not fear, that she may experience “the risen life” or the new life that has become hers through His Resurrection... saying to her “Rise up, my neighbor” (Song 2:10), do not fear. Trust, I have overcome the world and all its evils and death with all its authority.

2.12.1.en: Origen comments on the call of Christ to His betrothed, saying: [He says this to her to show her how fitting it is for her to despise the nets that the enemy set in the way, and not to fear the snares when she sees them torn by Him].

2.12.2.en: He calls her with authority to rise to cleave to Him and become His gentle dove, bearing the fruits of the Resurrection in her life, saying to her:

2.12.3.en: “Rise up, my neighbor, my fair one, my dove, and come away.

2.12.4.en: For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone.

2.12.5.en: The flowers appear on the earth; the time of pruning is come, and the voice of the Turtle-dove is heard in our land.

2.12.6.en: The fig tree putteth forth her green figs, and the vines with the tender grape give forth their smell” [10-13].

2.12.7.en: It is a call to the first resurrection, the resurrection of the human soul in Christ Jesus from the death of sin and its rising above bodily sensations and earthly lusts, so that she lives according to the Spirit and not the flesh.

2.12.8.en: Origen comments on this text, saying: [The Word of God is speaking just now with the beautiful noble soul, to whom He appears through her bodily senses—that is, through her reading Holy Scripture and her listening to teaching—as from windows, through which (the Word of God) appears as a tall and great person speaking to her the preceding words, and bending toward her calls her to rise and go out of the realm of the bodily senses, and cease to remain within the realm of the body, so she deserves to hear the voice: “Ye are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit” (Rom 8:9).

2.12.9.en: The Word of God would not have called her His neighbor and united with her and become one spirit with her (1 Cor 6:17), nor called her beautiful, had He not seen her image renewed day by day (2 Cor 4:16). And He would not have seen her able to receive the Holy Spirit who descended on Jesus at the Jordan in the form of a dove (Mt 3:6), nor called her “His dove,” had she not perceived the love of the Word of God and longed to go forth to Him swiftly while saying: “Oh that I had wings like a dove! for then would I fly away, and be at rest” (Ps 55:6). I fly with my affections, I fly with my spiritual perceptions, and I rest when I perceive the treasures of His wisdom and knowledge (Col 2:3).

2.12.10.en: It seems to me that just as those who receive the death of Christ and mortify their members which are upon the earth become partakers in the likeness of His death (Col 3:5; Rom 6:5), so also those who receive the power of the Holy Spirit and are sanctified by Him and are filled with His gifts become doves, in His likeness as He appeared in the form of a dove. They are lifted by the two wings of the Holy Spirit and fly, released from earthly and sensible things to the heavenly places.

2.12.11.en: And to show that the time has become suitable for the realization of these things, He intervenes in a logical way, saying: “For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone.” For the soul does not become one with the Word of God and unite with Him unless such a time passes, that is, every winter of her personal disturbances and the storms of her vices pass away, so that she is no longer shaken nor “carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph 4:14). When all these things pass from the soul, and the storms of lusts flee from her, the flowers of the virtues can begin to appear within her, and the time of pruning comes... Then also “the voice of the turtle-dove” is heard, which certainly refers to the wisdom that the one delegated by the “Word” speaks among the perfect, “the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom” (1 Cor 2:6).

2.12.12.en: And the mention of the Turtle-dove points to this fact: this bird spends its life in the most hidden and remote places away from the crowds. It loves the mountainous deserts or the hidden regions in the forests, and is always found far from the multitudes, a stranger to the crowds.

2.12.13.en: And what else suits this time and its delights?

2.12.14.en: He says: “The fig tree putteth forth her green figs,” for the spiritual man whom the fig tree signifies has not yet borne the fruits of the Spirit: love, joy, peace and the rest of these things (Gal 5:22), but has now begun to bear the unripe figs (the small buds).

2.12.15.en: Truly the trees in their various kinds are understood in the Church generally as a symbol of the souls of the believers, for it was written of them: “Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up” (Mt 15:13). And also Paul, who calls himself “a labourer together with God” in His vineyard (1 Cor 3:9), says: “I have planted, Apollos watered” (1 Cor 3:6). And the Lord Himself says in the Gospel: “Make the tree good, and his fruit good” (Mt 12:33). Thus since the trees in their various kinds are understood in the Church as the souls of the believers, the multiplicity of their kinds symbolizes the different powers and varied virtues of these souls.

2.12.16.en: Therefore there is in the soul the fig tree that brings forth its green figs, as there is the vine that brings forth its tender grapes and gives forth its sweet smell. And the Husbandman is the heavenly Father, who prunes the vine that it may bring forth more fruit (Jn 15:1)....

2.12.17.en: And the wonder is that while He calls her to the experience of the Resurrection, saying to her “Rise up,” He says to her “the time of pruning is come,” that is, the time of pruning the vineyard, which refers to crucifixion and suffering... where He removes from her the branches of the works of her old man and the temporal carnal thoughts so that she may bring forth more spiritual fruit bearing heavenly marks! He brings her into sufferings and the Cross that she may bear the fruit of the Resurrection. He separates her from the winter of the biting coldness of the spirit to bring her into the spring of the new risen life in Christ Jesus.

2.12.18.en: We can also see this call to the Resurrection directed to the whole world... to Jews and Gentiles, for the fig tree refers to the Law, so that by the descent of the Word to the world the Law is no longer understood through the killing letter but we were given to understand it spiritually...

2.12.19.en: So the Jews who accepted the Lord Christ bore the fruit of the Spirit and their hearts were enlarged with love toward all humanity. The Law was no longer for them a cause of pride and arrogance over the Gentiles as they had been before... therefore He says “the fig tree putteth forth her green figs.” And He also says: “the time of pruning is come,” that is, pruning of the vine, for if the vine referred in the Old Testament to the Jewish people, then its arrogant branches must be pruned so that it may receive the membership of the community of the Gentiles with it, and the sweet fragrance of Christ spreads to fill the whole world. The vine must be pruned of temporal earthly concepts that it may have spiritual heavenly perceptions.

2.13.s.en: The Resurrection: going out from coldness to warmth:

2.13.0.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa sees that this spring in which the flowers appeared and the fig tree put forth its green figs and the fragrance of the vine blossoms spread is the work of God, as the psalmist says: “The summer and the spring thou hast made them” (Ps 73:17). The winter of biting cold had ended and spring came with its warmth. In the winter man was in the coldness of idolatry; his changing nature had turned into the nature of the inanimate things he worshiped. For just as those who look to the true God receive the characteristics of the divine nature within them, so those who look to the vanity of idols are turned themselves into the very things they look at, becoming stones, not men. By worshiping idols they became immobile stone unable to progress... Therefore “the Sun of Righteousness” rose in this biting winter and spring came. The south wind removed this stiffness, and with the appearance of the rays of the sun warmth prevailed over everything on which the rays fell...
